title: Putting Greens in the Grand Strand | TIMELESS Grass & Greens
description: Backyard putting greens on the Grand Strand. See what Barefoot, Dye Estates, River Hills, Sea Trail and Brunswick Plantation rules say, then book a free visit.
h1: Add a backyard green that fits your community’s rules.
lede: Practice putts behind the house, no tee time needed. Golf communities here give different written answers on artificial turf, from greens allowed behind the house to no artificial grass at all. Check yours first. Then we measure, check the ground and draw a custom layout you approve before work starts.
wins: See what your community’s written rule says
A layout you can attach to your application
Contours and drainage planned for your lot

answer.question: Can I put an artificial putting green in a Grand Strand golf community?
answer.answer: It depends on your community. Dye Estates at Barefoot Resort allows putting greens behind the house. Barefoot’s master guidelines prohibit artificial turf, and Brunswick Plantation’s standards say no artificial grass is permitted. River Hills and Sea Trail limit green space or built-upon area, so ask how a green counts. Get your committee’s answer in writing, then call 303-349-2368 for a free visit.

blocks.h2: At Barefoot, your neighborhood decides which rule you start from.
paras: Barefoot Resort’s master architectural guidelines, revised June 1, 2025, say “Artificial Turf & Vegetation are prohibited,” and repeat it under landscaping. The same guidelines give Leatherleaf and Dye Estates their own review committees, with “primary responsibility for review and approval of applications” in those neighborhoods.

Dye Estates’ own guidelines, version 5.4, effective March 20, 2023, make an exception: “With the exception of putting greens, no artificial grass, plants, or other artificial vegetation shall be placed or maintained on the exterior of any Lot unless approved by the ARC.” Greens must sit to the rear of the house, and the limit of 40 percent impervious lot surface applies to them. A backyard green is listed among minor backyard changes of 500 square feet or less that need no application. You still follow the committee’s guidance, and that exception doesn’t cover new home construction. Because the master guidelines still list artificial turf as prohibited, ask the Dye Estates committee to confirm your green in writing.

Leatherleaf’s 2024 guidelines don’t mention artificial turf. They require committee approval for changes to an approved landscape plan, except minor ones, so ask the Leatherleaf committee whether your green counts as minor. Anywhere else in Barefoot, start from the master prohibition.

blocks.h2: At River Hills, fit the green around your green-space and sod rules.
paras: River Hills’ ARB standards manual, Revision 9 of November 9, 2021, says anyone who wants to build or alter improvements or landscaping “must submit a request for approval to the ARB.” At least 30 percent of the total site must be “pervious, open, landscaped space.” Each lot must also keep “a sodded area from curbside to a minimum of 50 percent of side dimension of residence,” in an approved sod such as St. Augustine, Centipede, Bermuda or Zoysia.

The manual doesn’t say whether a green counts as landscaped space. Take your layout to the ARB and ask, and plan the green outside the required sodded area. Our Little River page covers green sizes for patio-home and larger lots.

blocks.h2: At Sea Trail, ask how a green counts against your built-upon area.
paras: Sea Trail Master Association keeps its current documents behind a login, so ask the administrator for the current standards first. The publicly posted standards, revised and effective March 21, 2019, limit each lot’s built-upon area to the amount shown on a stormwater master plan approved by the State of North Carolina. Their list of what counts names structures, asphalt, concrete, gravel, brick, stone, slate and coquina.

Turf isn’t on that list, but a green is shaped on a compacted base, so ask whether the committee counts the turf, the base or neither. The 2019 standards also require “a minimum of 40% sodden area” in the front yard landscaped area, and lots within a CAMA Area of Environmental Concern may have their built-upon allowance reduced. Check both before you pick a spot.

blocks.h2: Brunswick Plantation bars artificial grass. Ocean Ridge posts no standards.
paras: Brunswick Plantation’s design standards are the file “ASC Standards (10.31.2022) update 8.14.2026.pdf” on the POA’s documents page. Its minimum planting requirements say lawn areas must be sodded with centipede, a similar zoysia, Bermuda or St. Augustine, and end: “No Artificial grass is permitted.” The rule doesn’t name putting greens, so before you pay for a design, ask the Architectural Standards Committee in writing whether it covers a green behind the house.

Ocean Ridge Master Association lists an Architectural Standards Committee on its community page but posts no standards there. Ask the committee for the current document before you choose a shape or size.

blocks.h2: A green’s contours are grading, and these communities have rules for it.
paras: The breaks in a green are shaped into the ground under the turf. Barefoot’s master guidelines send major grading changes such as berms and mounds for review and say “Water cannot be directed to flow onto a neighboring property.” Brunswick Plantation requires committee approval for fill, land shaping and drainage, and landscape submittals must show contours “with arrows indicating the direction of water flow.” River Hills keeps topographic changes inside your lot, meeting neighbors at natural grade. Sea Trail’s tree-preservation rules ask that the committee be told of all plans for land filling, shaping and drainage, and its run-off section cites State requirements to control run-off on your own property.

On the free visit, we measure, check the ground and look at where water leaves your yard now. Then we draw a custom layout you approve before work starts, ready to attach to your application, and build the base for your soil. Our Myrtle Beach page explains how the ground changes across the city. If an old or flooded green has to come out first, see turf replacement on the Grand Strand.

faq.q: Can I replace an old green where the rules now ban turf?
faq.a: Ask the committee in writing whether replacing an existing green needs a new application under the current rule. If it’s allowed, we remove the old turf, rebuild the base where it needs it and lay a new green to a layout you approve.

faq.q: My community isn’t listed here. What should I ask?
faq.a: Ask your architectural committee for its current guidelines and recorded covenants. Then ask in writing whether a putting green is allowed, where on the lot it can go, whether it needs an application and how it counts toward any impervious or green-space limit.

faq.q: What should I bring to the free visit?
faq.a: Bring your community’s current architectural document and any written answer from the committee, your survey or plot plan, any storm water worksheet on file and photos of where water sits after heavy rain. We use them to draw a layout that fits your lot’s limits.
